title: telc Deutsch B1 Grammar Practice
purpose: Original daily grammar quiz material for telc Deutsch B1 preparation.
content_policy: Rules and examples are original. External sources define coverage and exam alignment; no source exercises are reproduced.

scope: complete A1 and A2 foundation coverage
detailed rule explanations at A1, A2, and B1
one-to-one memory aids for every grammar topic
reference pages with rule-specific worked examples for every grammar topic
review.generated_practice_policy: Supplemental cards are derived from the rule library, detailed notes, and pre-existing reviewed examples. Each topic is brought to a minimum of ten direct cards with rotating task types and difficulty levels.

sources.title: Zertifikat Deutsch / telc Deutsch B1: current exam structure
Auf jeden Fall! Deutsch B1 Lehrerhandbuch

design_notes: Most cards use everyday contexts typical of B1 communication.
Production cards train connected writing and speaking, not recognition alone.
Distractors target frequent learner errors in case, agreement, tense, and word order.

cumulative_level_system.principle: B1 performance depends on automatic A1 and A2 grammar. Foundation cards remain in daily rotation and multi-rule cards combine rules across levels.

levels.A1: Form accurate simple clauses, questions, noun phrases, and basic past statements.
levels.A2: Connect clauses, control objects and pronouns, narrate, and describe relationships between ideas.
levels.B1: Combine structures flexibly to explain, justify, compare, narrate, hypothesize, and interact.

cumulative_level_system.unlock_rule: A learner may study B1 cards immediately, but weak A1/A2 dependencies are automatically inserted after related B1 errors.
cumulative_level_system.multi_rule_error_policy: When a multi-rule card is wrong, schedule one foundation card for every failed rule_id before repeating the integrated card.
diagnostic_cycle: Attempt the integrated card without hints.
Compare each reasoning step, not only the final answer.
Complete one basic and one intermediate card for each failed A1/A2 dependency.
Complete one related B1 single-topic card.
Retry the integrated card after at least one other card.
Schedule it for the next day if any reasoning step is still uncertain.

rule_library.rule_en: A German main clause keeps the finite verb in position 2. If another element comes first, the subject follows the verb.
rule_library.form: Element 1 + finite verb + subject + ...
rule_library.common_error: Putting both a time phrase and the subject before the verb.

rule_library.rule_en: Subordinating conjunctions send the finite verb to the end of their clause.
rule_library.form: conjunction + subject + ... + finite verb
rule_library.common_error: Keeping main-clause word order after weil, dass, obwohl, or wenn.

rule_library.rule_en: Weil introduces a subordinate reason, denn coordinates a reason, and deshalb introduces a consequence.
rule_library.form: weil + verb-final; denn + V2; deshalb + verb + subject
rule_library.common_error: Using deshalb to introduce a reason instead of a result.

rule_library.rule_en: Obwohl introduces an unexpected contrast; trotzdem introduces the resulting main clause; trotz is a preposition.
rule_library.form: obwohl + clause; trotzdem + V2; trotz + genitive
rule_library.common_error: Using obwohl and aber together.

rule_library.rule_en: Use um ... zu for one shared subject and damit when the clauses have different subjects.
rule_library.form: um + ... + zu-infinitive; damit + verb-final
rule_library.common_error: Using um ... zu even though the second action has its own subject.

rule_library.rule_en: Paired connectors link parallel words or clauses and express addition, alternatives, negation, or contrast.
rule_library.form: sowohl ... als auch; entweder ... oder; weder ... noch; zwar ... aber
rule_library.common_error: Mixing halves from different connector pairs.

rule_library.rule_en: Temporal conjunctions show whether events are simultaneous, repeated, earlier, later, or ongoing.
rule_library.form: als/wenn/während/nachdem/bevor/seitdem + verb-final
rule_library.common_error: Using als for repeated events or nachdem without a clear sequence.

rule_library.rule_en: Indirect yes/no questions use ob; indirect information questions retain the question word. The verb is final.
rule_library.form: ..., ob/wann/warum + subject + ... + verb
rule_library.common_error: Using direct-question inversion inside the indirect question.

rule_library.rule_en: The antecedent determines gender and number; the pronoun's role inside the relative clause determines case.
rule_library.form: noun, relative pronoun + ... + verb
rule_library.common_error: Choosing the case from the main clause instead of the relative clause.

rule_library.rule_en: Many verbs, nouns, and adjective expressions take zu + infinitive; separable prefixes place zu inside the verb.
rule_library.form: zu lernen; anzufangen; abzugeben
rule_library.common_error: Adding zu after modal verbs or placing it before a separable verb.

rule_library.rule_en: Konjunktiv II expresses polite requests, advice, wishes, and unreal conditions.
rule_library.form: hätte/wäre/könnte or würde + infinitive
rule_library.common_error: Using würde with hätte, wäre, or modal verbs when their own forms are clearer.

rule_library.rule_en: The process passive focuses on an action; the state passive focuses on its result.
rule_library.form: werden + Partizip II; sein + Partizip II
rule_library.common_error: Confusing wird geschlossen with ist geschlossen.

rule_library.rule_en: Perfekt dominates conversation, Präteritum is common in writing and with sein/haben/modals, and Plusquamperfekt marks an earlier past.
rule_library.form: hat gemacht; war/musste; hatte gemacht
rule_library.common_error: Choosing the wrong auxiliary or failing to distinguish two past times.

rule_library.rule_en: Futur I expresses future events or assumptions; present tense with a time marker often expresses the future too.
rule_library.form: werden + infinitive
rule_library.common_error: Using Futur I in every future sentence or confusing werden with würden.

rule_library.rule_en: Modal verbs modify ability, necessity, permission, intention, or reported advice and send the main infinitive to the end.
rule_library.form: subject + modal + ... + infinitive
rule_library.common_error: Adding zu before the infinitive or confusing nicht müssen with nicht dürfen.

rule_library.rule_en: Case marks a noun phrase's role and is also governed by verbs and prepositions.
rule_library.form: nominative subject; accusative object; dative recipient
rule_library.common_error: Selecting case by word order rather than grammatical function.

rule_library.rule_en: Attributive adjective endings show gender, case, and number together with the preceding determiner.
rule_library.form: der gute; ein guter; gutes Brot
rule_library.common_error: Using an uninflected adjective before a noun.

rule_library.rule_en: Genitive expresses possession and follows several formal prepositions such as wegen, trotz, and während.
rule_library.form: das Auto meines Bruders; wegen des Wetters
rule_library.common_error: Omitting -(e)s on masculine and neuter genitive nouns.

rule_library.rule_en: Most weak masculine nouns add -n or -en in every singular case except nominative.
rule_library.form: der Student; den/dem/des Studenten
rule_library.common_error: Leaving the accusative or dative form without -n/-en.

rule_library.rule_en: Many German verbs require a fixed preposition and case that must be learned with the verb.
rule_library.form: warten auf + accusative; teilnehmen an + dative
rule_library.common_error: Translating the preposition directly from English.

rule_library.rule_en: Use da(r)+preposition for things and preposition + personal pronoun for people; questions use wo(r)+preposition.
rule_library.form: darauf/worauf; auf ihn/auf wen
rule_library.common_error: Using davon or worauf to refer to a person.

rule_library.rule_en: Kein negates nouns with an indefinite or zero article; nicht negates verbs, adjectives, definite nouns, or selected sentence parts.
rule_library.form: kein Geld; nicht kommen; nicht das Auto
rule_library.common_error: Using nicht directly before every noun.

rule_library.rule_en: Use so ... wie for equality and comparative + als for inequality.
rule_library.form: so schnell wie; schneller als
rule_library.common_error: Using wie after a comparative.

rule_library.rule_en: Partizip I has active simultaneous meaning; Partizip II usually has completed or passive meaning when used adjectivally.
rule_library.form: das lachende Kind; die geschlossene Tür
rule_library.common_error: Forgetting the adjective ending on the participle.

rule_library.rule_en: Verbs and adjectives can become nouns and are then capitalized.
rule_library.form: das Lesen; beim Kochen; die Freundlichkeit
rule_library.common_error: Writing a nominalized infinitive with a lowercase letter.

rule_library.rule_en: Prefixes, suffixes, and compounds create predictable families of nouns and adjectives.
rule_library.form: -ung, -heit, -keit, -bar, -lich, un-
rule_library.common_error: Assuming every English-looking suffix has the same German meaning.

rule_library.rule_en: Lassen + bare infinitive expresses permission, causation, or arranging a service.
rule_library.form: Ich lasse das reparieren; habe schneiden lassen
rule_library.common_error: Adding zu or using a participle instead of the double infinitive in Perfekt.

rule_library.rule_en: Everyday reports often use dass; formal reports use Konjunktiv I to mark information as reported.
rule_library.form: Sie sagt, dass ...; er sei/habe ...
rule_library.common_error: Failing to adjust pronouns or using main-clause word order after dass.

rule_library.rule_en: Ordinals use -te up to 19 and -ste from 20, then take adjective endings.
rule_library.form: der dritte; am einundzwanzigsten
rule_library.common_error: Forgetting the dative -n after am.

rule_library.rule_en: Werden expresses change, forms Futur I, and serves as the auxiliary of the process passive.
rule_library.form: wird müde; wird kommen; wird gemacht
rule_library.common_error: Confusing the three functions or forming Perfekt with haben.

rule_library.rule_en: Possessive determiners identify the owner but their endings agree with the possessed noun.
rule_library.form: mein Bruder; meine Tasche; mit meinem Bruder
rule_library.common_error: Choosing the ending based on the owner's gender.

rule_library.rule_en: Nouns formed with the diminutive suffix -chen or -lein are neuter, often gain an umlaut, and have no plural ending.
rule_library.form: das Häuschen; die Häuschen
rule_library.common_error: Using natural gender instead of neuter grammatical gender.

rule_library.rule_en: Wo can refer to places; was follows alles, etwas, nichts, das, and substantivized superlatives.
rule_library.form: die Stadt, wo ...; alles, was ...
rule_library.common_error: Using das after alles or a substantivized superlative.

rule_library.rule_en: Adversative connectors contrast or correct ideas using different clause structures.
rule_library.form: aber/sondern + V2; dagegen + verb-subject; während + verb-final
rule_library.common_error: Using sondern without a preceding negation.

rule_library.rule_en: Temporal prepositions specify points, durations, starts, and endpoints and govern particular cases.
rule_library.form: am Montag; im Mai; seit einem Jahr; bis Freitag
rule_library.common_error: Mixing seit for an ongoing period with vor for a completed past point.

rule_library.rule_en: The subject pronoun determines the present-tense verb ending. Regular endings are -e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en.
rule_library.form: ich lerne; du lernst; er lernt; wir lernen; ihr lernt; sie/Sie lernen
rule_library.common_error: Using the infinitive with a singular subject or confusing lowercase sie with formal Sie.
details: The stem is usually the infinitive minus -en.
Some stems require spelling adjustments or a vowel change.
Formal Sie always uses the same form as plural sie and is capitalized.

rule_library.rule_en: W-questions begin with a question word and keep the finite verb second; yes/no questions begin with the finite verb.
rule_library.form: Wo wohnst du?; Kommst du morgen?
rule_library.common_error: Keeping statement order in a yes/no question.
details: Wer asks for a person as subject; wen/wem mark other cases.
Was asks for a thing or action.
Question words count as position 1.

rule_library.rule_en: Every noun has grammatical gender and should be learned with its article and plural.
rule_library.form: der Tisch/die Tische; die Lampe/die Lampen; das Kind/die Kinder
rule_library.common_error: Guessing gender from English or adding one universal plural ending.
details: All German nouns are capitalized.
Plural articles are always die in nominative and accusative.
Plural formation may use -e, -er, -(e)n, -s, no ending, and sometimes an umlaut.

rule_library.rule_en: Nominative marks the subject; accusative commonly marks the direct object. Only masculine articles visibly change in the simplest patterns.
rule_library.form: der/ein Mann -> den/einen Mann
rule_library.common_error: Changing every accusative article or failing to change masculine der/ein.
details: Ask who performs the action for nominative.
Ask whom/what the action directly affects for accusative.
Feminine, neuter, and plural definite articles look the same in nominative and accusative.

rule_library.rule_en: Kein negates an indefinite or articleless noun; nicht negates verbs, adjectives, definite noun phrases, or specific elements.
rule_library.form: kein Auto; nicht teuer; heute nicht
rule_library.common_error: Using nicht before an indefinite noun.
details: Kein takes ein-word endings.
Nicht normally stands before the element it specifically negates.
Whole-clause nicht often appears late in the middle field.

rule_library.rule_en: Possessive determiners identify an owner, but their endings agree with the possessed noun.
rule_library.form: mein Bruder; meine Schwester; mein Kind
rule_library.common_error: Choosing the ending from the owner's gender.
details: mein corresponds to ich, dein to du, sein to er/es, ihr to sie, unser to wir, euer to ihr, Ihr to formal Sie.
They decline like ein.
Euer often drops an internal e before an ending: eure.

rule_library.rule_en: The finite verb occupies position 2 in a statement; one whole element may occupy position 1.
rule_library.form: Ich arbeite heute.; Heute arbeite ich.
rule_library.common_error: Counting individual words instead of sentence elements.
details: The subject is often first but does not have to be.
When time or place is first, subject-verb inversion follows.
The finite verb is the conjugated part.

rule_library.rule_en: A separable prefix moves to the clause end while the conjugated stem stays in position 2.
rule_library.form: Ich rufe dich an.
rule_library.common_error: Conjugating the whole infinitive in one position.
details: Common prefixes include an-, auf-, ein-, mit-, vor-, and zurück-.
The prefix is stressed in speech.
Modal verbs create another bracket: Ich muss anrufen.

rule_library.rule_en: Clock times, dates, and quantities use fixed patterns that combine numbers with temporal prepositions.
rule_library.form: um acht Uhr; am dritten Mai; von neun bis elf
rule_library.common_error: Using am for a clock time or forgetting ordinal endings in dates.
details: Um marks a precise clock time.
Am is used with weekdays and dates.
Im is used with months, seasons, and years when appropriate.

rule_library.rule_en: Basic prepositions encode origin, destination, location, accompaniment, and time, and govern a fixed case.
rule_library.form: aus Berlin; nach Köln; bei Anna; mit dem Bus; am Montag
rule_library.common_error: Translating English prepositions word for word.
details: Nach is used for most cities/countries without an article and for nach Hause.
In is used with countries that have an article.
Aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, and zu take dative.

rule_library.rule_en: Dative marks many recipients and follows specific verbs and prepositions.
rule_library.form: dem Mann; der Frau; dem Kind; den Kindern
rule_library.common_error: Forgetting plural -n or using accusative after mit.
details: Dative articles are dem, der, dem, den.
Dative plural nouns usually add -n when possible.
Common dative verbs include helfen, danken, gefallen, and gehören.

rule_library.rule_en: Two-way prepositions take dative for location and accusative for a destination or change of position.
rule_library.form: Das Bild hängt an der Wand.; Ich hänge es an die Wand.
rule_library.common_error: Choosing case from movement alone rather than the wo/wohin distinction.
details: The set is an, auf, hinter, in, neben, über, unter, vor, zwischen.
Wo? normally takes dative.
Wohin? normally takes accusative.

rule_library.rule_en: Modal verbs express ability, necessity, permission, intention, or advice and combine with a final bare infinitive.
rule_library.form: Ich kann kommen.; Du musst lernen.
rule_library.common_error: Adding zu before the infinitive.
details: The singular forms are often irregular.
The modal is finite and occupies position 2.
The content verb remains infinitive at the clause end.

rule_library.rule_en: The imperative gives instructions or requests and has different du, ihr, and Sie forms.
rule_library.form: Komm!; Kommt!; Kommen Sie!
rule_library.common_error: Including du in a normal imperative or forgetting Sie in the formal form.
details: Du imperative usually uses the stem.
Ihr imperative equals the present ihr form without ihr.
Formal imperative is infinitive-form verb + Sie.

rule_library.rule_en: Comparatives usually add -er, superlatives use am ...-sten, equality uses wie, and inequality uses als.
rule_library.form: schneller als; so schnell wie; am schnellsten
rule_library.common_error: Using wie after a comparative.
details: Some common forms are irregular: gut-besser-am besten, viel-mehr-am meisten.
Many one-syllable adjectives add an umlaut.
Attributive superlatives take adjective endings.

rule_library.rule_en: The conversational past uses haben or sein plus Partizip II at the clause end.
rule_library.form: Ich habe gelernt.; Ich bin gefahren.
rule_library.common_error: Choosing the wrong auxiliary or placing the participle beside it.
details: Most verbs use haben.
Movement with a destination and change-of-state verbs often use sein.
Regular participles commonly use ge- + stem + -t; inseparable verbs omit ge-.

rule_library.rule_en: An adjective before a noun takes an ending; a predicative adjective after sein remains unchanged.
rule_library.form: ein rotes Auto; das Auto ist rot
rule_library.common_error: Adding an ending after sein or omitting it before a noun.
details: After definite articles, -e and -en dominate.
After ein-words, the adjective sometimes carries missing gender/case information.
Article, adjective, and noun form one case-marked phrase.

rule_library.rule_en: Personal pronouns change form by case.
rule_library.form: mich/mir; dich/dir; ihn/ihm; sie/ihr; es/ihm
rule_library.common_error: Using subject pronouns as objects.
details: Accusative answers wen/was.
Dative answers wem.
Short pronouns normally appear earlier than full noun objects.

rule_library.rule_en: German combines words productively; the final component determines a compound noun's gender.
rule_library.form: die Arbeit + das Zimmer = das Arbeitszimmer
rule_library.common_error: Choosing the article from the first component.
details: Compounds are written as one word.
Linking sounds such as -s- may appear.
Knowing components helps decode unfamiliar vocabulary.

rule_library.rule_en: Hätte and wäre express simple wishes and polite preferences.
rule_library.form: Ich hätte gern ...; Ich wäre gern ...
rule_library.common_error: Using hatte/war when the meaning is a present wish.
details: Hätte is used with desired things.
Wäre is used with states, identities, or locations.
Gern softens and completes the common wish frame.

rule_library.rule_en: Weil gives a reason and dass introduces reported content or a fact; both send the finite verb to the end.
rule_library.form: ..., weil ich krank bin.; Ich weiß, dass er kommt.
rule_library.common_error: Keeping verb-second order inside the subordinate clause.
details: A preceding subordinate clause occupies position 1 of the main clause.
A comma separates main and subordinate clauses.
With a modal, the content infinitive precedes the finite modal at the end.

rule_library.rule_en: Indirect yes/no questions use ob; indirect information questions retain their W-word and use verb-final order.
rule_library.form: Ich frage, ob er kommt.; Weißt du, wann es beginnt?
rule_library.common_error: Using dass for a yes/no question or retaining direct-question inversion.
details: The clause is embedded after verbs such as wissen, fragen, and sagen können.
A polite frame can precede it: Können Sie mir sagen ...?
The question mark depends on the whole sentence, not the embedded clause alone.

rule_library.rule_en: Article and adjective endings share the job of marking gender, number, and case.
rule_library.form: der nette Mann; ein netter Mann; netter Mann
rule_library.common_error: Memorizing endings without first identifying article type and case.
details: After definite articles, adjectives mostly use -e or -en.
After ein-words, the adjective supplies missing strong information.
Without an article, the adjective usually carries strong case endings.

rule_library.rule_en: A reflexive pronoun refers back to the subject and may be accusative or dative.
rule_library.form: Ich freue mich.; Ich wasche mir die Hände.
rule_library.common_error: Always using accusative mich/dich even when another accusative object is present.
details: Accusative forms differ only in first and second person.
With a body part or other direct object, the reflexive pronoun is often dative.
Some verbs are obligatorily reflexive; others change meaning when reflexive.

rule_library.rule_en: Many verbs and adjectives require a fixed preposition and case that form one learnable pattern.
rule_library.form: warten auf + Akk.; zufrieden mit + Dat.
rule_library.common_error: Selecting the preposition by translating from English.
details: Learn the verb/adjective, preposition, and case together.
The prepositional complement may be a noun, pronoun, da-compound, or clause.
Person questions use preposition + wen/wem.

rule_library.rule_en: Relative clauses describe a noun; the antecedent gives gender/number and the pronoun's clause role gives case.
rule_library.form: der Mann, der ...; den Mann, den ...; die Frau, der ...
rule_library.common_error: Choosing the relative pronoun from the main-clause case.
details: The relative clause is separated by commas.
Its finite verb is final.
A governing preposition stands before the relative pronoun.

rule_library.rule_en: Präteritum narrates past events and is especially common with sein, haben, modal verbs, and in written stories.
rule_library.form: war, hatte, konnte, musste, machte, ging
rule_library.common_error: Mixing present and past forms or applying regular -te to strong verbs.
details: Regular verbs use stem + -te endings.
Strong verbs change their stem and do not use -te.
Mixed verbs combine a stem change with -te, such as dachte and brachte.

rule_library.rule_en: With two objects, pronouns tend to precede full nouns; when both are pronouns, accusative normally precedes dative.
rule_library.form: Ich gebe dem Kind das Buch.; Ich gebe es ihm.
rule_library.common_error: Applying one fixed dative-before-accusative order even when pronouns are used.
details: Two full nouns commonly use dative before accusative.
A pronoun normally precedes a noun object.
Two pronouns normally use accusative before dative.

rule_library.rule_en: Position verbs and direction verbs pair with different cases and often different verb choices.
rule_library.form: Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch.; Ich lege es auf den Tisch.
rule_library.common_error: Using liegen/stehen for placing something or choosing dative for a destination.
details: liegen/stehen/sitzen describe position.
legen/stellen/setzen describe placing or direction.
Two-way prepositions take dative for wo and accusative for wohin.

rule_library.rule_en: Indefinite pronouns refer to nonspecific people/things; impersonal expressions use es or man without a concrete agent.
rule_library.form: jemand, niemand, etwas, nichts; man sagt; es regnet
rule_library.common_error: Treating man as the noun Mann or omitting required impersonal es.
details: Man always takes a third-person singular verb.
Jemand and niemand may receive case endings.
Weather and certain fixed expressions require es.

rule_library.rule_en: The process passive uses werden + Partizip II and focuses on what happens rather than who acts.
rule_library.form: Das Paket wird geliefert.; Die Pakete wurden geliefert.
rule_library.common_error: Using sein when describing an action or forgetting agreement on werden.
details: The active accusative object becomes the passive nominative subject.
The agent can be omitted or introduced with von.
Tense is marked on werden.

rule_library.rule_en: Purpose is expressed with um ... zu when the subject is shared and damit when the purpose clause has its own subject.
rule_library.form: Ich lerne, um zu bestehen.; Ich erkläre es, damit du es verstehst.
rule_library.common_error: Using um ... zu with a different subject.
details: The zu-infinitive stands at the end.
Separable verbs insert zu between prefix and stem.
Damit introduces a finite subordinate clause.

rule_library.rule_en: Coordinating and paired connectors join equal elements without changing basic main-clause word order.
rule_library.form: aber, oder, denn; sowohl ... als auch; entweder ... oder
rule_library.common_error: Sending the verb to the end after denn or aber.
details: Aber contrasts; oder offers alternatives; denn gives a reason.
Paired halves should connect grammatically parallel elements.
Weder ... noch negates both alternatives.

rule_library.rule_en: Da(r)- compounds refer to things; wo(r)- compounds ask about things. People use preposition + pronoun.
rule_library.form: darauf/worauf; mit ihm/mit wem
rule_library.common_error: Using da-compounds for people.
details: Insert r before a vowel-initial preposition: daran, darüber.
The required preposition comes from the verb or adjective.
A da-compound can anticipate a dass-clause or infinitive clause.

rule_library.rule_en: Genitive marks possession and relationships; proper names often add -s without an article.
rule_library.form: Annas Auto; das Auto meines Bruders
rule_library.common_error: Adding an apostrophe before a normal German genitive -s.
details: Names ending in s-sound commonly take an apostrophe only: Max' Auto.
Masculine and neuter common nouns often add -(e)s.
In informal speech, von + dative may replace genitive.

rule_library.rule_en: Suggestions use modal questions and frames; polite requests often use könnte/würde in Konjunktiv II.
rule_library.form: Wollen wir ...?; Wir könnten ...; Könnten Sie ...?
rule_library.common_error: Using a direct command when a cooperative or formal request is expected.
details: Wie wäre es mit + dative? introduces a suggestion.
Lass uns + infinitive is informal.
Könnten Sie ...? is a standard polite request.

rule_library.rule_en: The suffix -ung commonly turns a verb into a feminine action/result noun and may trigger spelling changes.
rule_library.form: entscheiden -> die Entscheidung; anmelden -> die Anmeldung
rule_library.common_error: Keeping the infinitive ending or assigning a non-feminine article.
details: All -ung nouns are feminine.
Separable prefixes stay attached in the noun.
Nominalization often supports formal, compact writing.

rule_library.rule_en: Exam sentences normally require several decisions in sequence: identify clause structure, locate finite verbs, determine verb government and case, inflect the noun phrase, then check tense, reference, and meaning.
rule_library.form: meaning -> clause type -> verb positions -> government/case -> endings -> final agreement check
rule_library.common_error: Solving only the visible blank while ignoring another rule elsewhere in the clause.
details: Read the entire sentence before choosing an answer.
Mark connectors and finite verbs first.
For each noun phrase, identify its governing verb or preposition and case.
Check whether pronouns, adjective endings, and verb agreement match.
Finally test whether tense and connector meaning fit the wider context.

memory_aids.tip_en: In a main-clause statement, think of the finite verb as glued to seat 2; moving something into seat 1 moves the subject, not the verb.
In a subordinate clause, the finite verb normally waits at the end; verb clusters with a replacement infinitive are an important exception.
Weil gives the cause with verb-final order; denn gives the cause with V2; deshalb points forward to the result.
Obwohl introduces the obstacle, trotzdem introduces what happens despite it, and trotz must stand before a noun phrase.
For the same doer, prefer um ... zu; a different doer requires damit plus a finite verb.
Learn each pair as an indivisible two-piece frame and make both sides grammatically parallel.
Use als for one past event or period, wenn for repeated events or conditions, and check the timeline before choosing nachdem or bevor.
Keep the question word, or use ob for yes/no, then park the verb at the end.
Look left for gender and number, but look inside the relative clause for case.
Zu sits immediately before a simple infinitive but slips between a separable prefix and its stem.
Unreal or extra-polite language wears an umlaut when possible: hätte, wäre, könnte.
For passive, ask whether the action is happening or the result is already true: werden presents the process, sein presents the state.
Perfekt is the usual conversational past, Präteritum is common in narration, and Plusquamperfekt steps one event further back.
A future time word often makes Präsens enough; use werden when prediction, intention, or assumption needs emphasis.
In a main-clause statement, the modal takes seat 2 and sends the action infinitive, without zu, to the end.
Ask who acts, what is affected, and to whom; then check whether the verb or preposition overrides that shortcut.
The article and adjective share one identification job: if the article says less, the adjective must say more.
Genitive links owners to possessions; masculine and neuter owners usually carry an extra -(e)s.
A weak masculine noun is bare only as nominative singular; everywhere else it puts on -(e)n.
Memorize verb, preposition, and case as one vocabulary item, such as warten auf + accusative.
Things become da- and questions about things become wo-; people keep the preposition plus pronoun.
Kein negates nouns with an indefinite or zero article; nicht negates other elements or the whole statement.
Equal partners use wie; a comparative difference crosses the line with als.
Partizip I is active and simultaneous; Partizip II is usually completed, resultative, or passive. Before a noun, both need an adjective ending.
If an action or quality behaves like a thing and can take an article, capitalize it.
Read a compound noun from the right: the final component controls its basic meaning, gender, and plural pattern.
After lassen, keep the second verb bare and final: Ich lasse das Auto reparieren, not zu reparieren.
Dass reports content neutrally; Konjunktiv I puts a visible 'reported, not guaranteed by me' label on it.
Use -te through nineteenth, -ste from twentieth, and then decline the ordinal like an adjective.
Werden plus an adjective or noun phrase means become, plus infinitive forms Futur I, and plus Partizip II forms process passive.
The possessive stem names the owner, but the ending behaves like ein and describes the possessed noun's case, gender, and number.
When -chen or -lein is a diminutive suffix, it always makes the resulting noun grammatically neuter.
Wo can point back to a place; was follows broad neuter ideas such as alles, nichts, das, or a substantivized superlative.
Aber contrasts, sondern corrects after a negation, dagegen triggers V2 inversion, and während sends its verb to the end.
Learn each time preposition with its question: wann, seit wann, wie lange, or bis wann.
For regular present-tense verbs, learn the core rhythm: ich -e, du -st, er/sie/es -t, wir/Sie -en, ihr -t; some stems insert an extra e.
W-word first and verb second; without a W-word, the verb takes first place.
Treat article, noun, and plural as one vocabulary package from the first day.
The masculine signal changes from der/ein to den/einen; most other basic article forms stay visibly unchanged.
Use kein for a noun with an indefinite or zero article; use nicht for verbs, adjectives, definite nouns, or a selected element.
Mein behaves like ein: choose the stem from the owner, then choose the ending from the possessed noun.
In a statement, count sentence elements, not words: the whole first element occupies one slot, then comes the finite verb.
In a main clause, the conjugated stem opens the sentence bracket and the separable prefix closes it.
Attach the matching frame to each number: um for clock time, am for dates/days, and vom ... bis for ranges.
Never learn a preposition alone; store it with one model phrase and its case.
Dative often answers wem, and plural dative adds -n unless the plural already ends in -n/-en or -s.
With a two-way preposition, ask wo for location and wohin for destination: wo takes dative, wohin accusative.
The modal is conjugated near the front; the meaning verb stays bare at the end.
For commands, du drops the pronoun, ihr also drops ihr, but formal Sie stays visible after the verb: Kommen Sie bitte.
Use so ... wie for equality, a comparative with als for inequality, and am plus -sten for the adverbial superlative.
In a main clause, build a bracket: conjugated haben/sein near the front and the participle at the end.
Before a noun, dress the adjective with an ending; after sein, leave it unchanged.
Ask wen/was for accusative and wem for dative before choosing mich/mir, ihn/ihm, or sie/ihr.
Read compounds from the right: the final noun is the boss and gives the whole word its article and core meaning.
Use hätte gern for a desired thing and wäre gern for a desired state, identity, or place.
Weil introduces a reason and dass introduces content; both normally close their clause with the finite verb.
Ob replaces yes/no inversion; a W-word remains, but both patterns send the verb to the end.
Identify case, gender, and article type first; only then choose the adjective ending.
If another accusative object is already present, the reflexive pronoun is often dative.
Store the whole chain as vocabulary: expression plus preposition plus case.
The noun outside gives gender and number; the verb or preposition inside gives case.
Regular verbs carry -te, strong verbs change their stem, and mixed verbs do both.
Pronouns rush ahead of nouns; when both objects are pronouns, accusative usually wins the race.
With two-way prepositions, position verbs answer wo with dative; placement verbs answer wohin with accusative.
Man means people in general and always takes a singular verb; es fills impersonal weather and fixed-expression slots.
Conjugate werden for tense and number, then place the action participle at the end.
For purpose clauses, one shared subject can use um ... zu; if the purpose has a different subject, use damit plus a finite verb.
Aber, oder, and denn connect equal clauses, so the following clause keeps normal V2 order.
Da points back and wo asks; add r before a vowel-initial preposition, as in daran and worüber.
German normally attaches genitive -s directly to a name; reserve the apostrophe for names already ending in an s-sound.
Move one step from command to question and another into Konjunktiv II to increase politeness.
When a verb forms a noun with -ung, the resulting noun is always feminine, so learn it with die.
Use the same five-pass scan every time: connector, verbs, government/case, endings/agreement, then meaning.

details: Position 1 is one sentence element, which may contain several words.
The finite verb remains position 2 even when the subject moves behind it.
Separable prefixes, infinitives, and participles form a right sentence bracket.
Inside the middle field, temporal-causal-modal-local is a useful neutral tendency, not an absolute law.
Subordinating conjunctions place the finite verb at the clause end.
Perfect and passive clusters normally place the nonfinite forms before the auxiliary.
With a modal replacement infinitive, the finite auxiliary may precede the double infinitive.
A subordinate clause placed first occupies position 1 and triggers main-clause inversion.
Weil introduces a verb-final reason clause.
Denn coordinates a normal verb-second reason clause.
Deshalb, deswegen, and daher introduce a consequence and trigger inversion when first.
Wegen and aufgrund package the cause as a noun phrase, usually with genitive in formal writing.
Obwohl presents a fact that would normally lead to a different result.
Trotzdem introduces the unexpected result as a main clause.
Trotz expresses concession as a prepositional phrase.
Do not pair obwohl with an additional aber in the main clause.
Um ... zu is used when the understood subject of the infinitive matches the main-clause subject.
Damit introduces a finite clause and allows a different subject.
Separable infinitives insert zu between prefix and stem.
Purpose differs from consequence: damit answers wozu, deshalb answers with what result.
Both halves should connect parallel grammatical units.
Sowohl ... als auch adds both; nicht nur ... sondern auch adds an emphasized second point.
Entweder ... oder offers alternatives; weder ... noch rejects both.
Zwar ... aber concedes the first statement and contrasts the second.
Als is used for a single past event or period; wenn covers repetition, conditions, present, and future.
Während marks simultaneity or contrast.
Bevor introduces the later action; nachdem introduces the earlier completed action.
Seitdem links a past starting point with a situation continuing to the reference time.
Ob introduces embedded yes/no questions.
A W-question retains its question word.
The embedded finite verb is final, while the outer clause follows its own sentence type.
Polite frames such as Könnten Sie mir sagen make the structure valuable in speaking and formal email.
The antecedent supplies gender and number, but the relative clause supplies case.
A governing preposition stands directly before the relative pronoun.
The finite verb is final and commas separate the clause.
Dessen and deren express possession; the following possessed noun normally has no article.
Zu-infinitives follow many verbs, nouns, and adjective expressions.
Modal verbs, lassen, and perception verbs normally use a bare infinitive.
Separable verbs insert zu; inseparable and -ieren verbs place zu before the whole infinitive.
An infinitive group is usually comma-separated when introduced by um, ohne, or statt or when clarity requires it.
Hätte, wäre, and modal forms are preferred to würde constructions.
Würde + infinitive is productive for many other verbs.
Present forms express wishes, politeness, advice, and unreal present conditions.
Past unreal meaning uses hätte/wäre + Partizip II in condition and result.
Process passive uses werden and focuses on the action.
State passive uses sein and focuses on the resulting condition.
The active accusative object becomes nominative; an agent or source can use von, while a means or cause can use durch.
With a modal, the clause ends Partizip II + werden; perfect passive uses worden, not geworden.
Perfekt is common in conversation, while Präteritum dominates written narration and common auxiliaries/modals.
Auxiliary choice in Perfekt depends on the verb and meaning.
Plusquamperfekt marks an event earlier than another past event.
Keep a narrative timeline consistent and use tense changes only when the time relationship changes.
Present tense plus a clear time phrase often expresses a planned future naturally.
Futur I uses werden + infinitive for prediction, promise, intention, or assumption.
Wohl and wahrscheinlich often signal assumption.
Futur II uses werden + Partizip II + haben/sein for completed future events or assumptions about the past.
The modal is finite and the content infinitive closes the clause.
Nicht müssen means no necessity, while nicht dürfen means prohibition.
Sollen can report another person's instruction or expectation.
Past modal perfect may use a replacement infinitive, but Präteritum is usually simpler at B1.
Case comes from syntactic role, verb government, or preposition.
Some verbs take two objects, typically a dative person and accusative thing.
Two-way prepositions distinguish location from destination.
Check article, adjective, noun, and pronoun forms as one connected case decision.
First identify case, gender, number, and determiner type.
Definite articles carry clear information, so adjectives mostly take weak -e/-en.
Ein-words leave some information for mixed adjective endings.
Without a determiner, strong adjective endings largely resemble definite-article endings.
Genitive marks possession and follows formal prepositions such as wegen, trotz, während, and aufgrund.
Masculine and neuter singular nouns often add -(e)s.
Proper names normally add -s without an apostrophe.
Relative possession uses dessen or deren according to the possessor, not the possessed item.
Weak masculine nouns take -(e)n in every singular case except nominative.
Typical groups include people ending in -e and international person nouns such as Student or Präsident.
The article still marks case normally.
A small mixed group such as Name adds -n in most cases and -ns in genitive.
Learn each verb together with its fixed preposition and case.
The complement may refer to a person, thing, or entire clause.
A person uses preposition + pronoun; a thing can use a da-compound.
Some verbs require two prepositional complements, such as sich bei jemandem über etwas beschweren.
Da(r)+preposition refers back to things, ideas, or clauses.
Wo(r)+preposition asks about things.
Insert r before a vowel: daran, darauf, darüber.
People require preposition + wen/wem or a personal pronoun instead.
Kein negates a noun phrase with an indefinite or zero article.
Nicht negates adjectives, verbs, definite noun phrases, prepositional phrases, or the whole proposition.
For focused negation, nicht stands directly before the contrasted element.
Avoid redundant double negation unless deliberately quoting nonstandard speech.
Equality uses so/genauso ... wie; inequality uses comparative + als.
The superlative is am ...-sten adverbially and takes adjective endings attributively.
Common forms such as gut, viel, gern, hoch, and nah are irregular.
Je ... desto/umso links two proportional changes and affects word order in both clauses.
Partizip I is infinitive + d and normally has active, simultaneous meaning.
Partizip II normally expresses completed, resulting, or passive meaning.
Used before a noun, either participle takes normal adjective endings.
Expanded participial attributes compress relative clauses but should remain readable at B1.
Nominalized infinitives are neuter and capitalized.
Suffixes such as -ung, -heit, and -keit create abstract nouns with predictable gender.
Nominal style can replace subordinate clauses with prepositional noun phrases.
Former objects often become genitive attributes or prepositional complements.
Prefixes can reverse, modify, or specify meaning; suffixes often signal word class and gender.
-ung, -heit, and -keit nouns are feminine; -chen nouns are neuter.
-bar often expresses possibility; un- often expresses an opposite.
Compounds inherit gender and core meaning from the final component.
Lassen + bare infinitive can express permission, causation, or arranging a service.
The affected person appears in accusative.
In Perfekt with another infinitive, use haben + infinitive + lassen.
Sich lassen + infinitive can express possibility, similar to a passive with können.
Everyday reports often use dass plus indicative.
Formal reporting uses Konjunktiv I to mark distance from the claim.
When Konjunktiv I equals indicative, Konjunktiv II may serve as a substitute.
Pronouns, possessives, time, and place expressions must shift to the reporter's perspective.
Ordinals 1-19 generally use -te; 20 and above use -ste.
They behave like adjectives and receive case endings.
Dates with am use dative -en.
Irregular stems include erste, dritte, siebte, and achte.
Werden + adjective/noun expresses change.
Werden + infinitive forms Futur I.
Werden + Partizip II forms process passive.
Perfect change uses ist geworden, while perfect passive uses ist ... worden.
The stem identifies the owner; the ending identifies the possessed noun's case, gender, and number.
They decline like ein-words.
Formal Ihr is always capitalized.
Possessives can stand independently, but endings then carry all noun-phrase information.
The diminutive suffixes -chen and -lein make every resulting noun neuter; a word that merely ends in the same letters need not follow this rule.
The base vowel often takes an umlaut when possible.
Singular and plural forms are identical.
Diminutives may express literal smallness, affection, or lexicalized meanings.
Wo can refer to a place, though preposition + relative pronoun is often more formal.
Was follows alles, etwas, nichts, das, and substantivized superlatives.
The relative clause remains verb-final.
Do not use was as a general replacement for ordinary gendered antecedents.
Aber coordinates a general contrast.
Sondern corrects a preceding negated element.
Dagegen and hingegen contrast statements and follow conjunctive-adverb word order.
Während can introduce a verb-final clause expressing contrast rather than time.
Um marks clock time; am marks days/dates; im marks months, seasons, and many years.
Seit + dative describes duration continuing from the past.
Vor + dative places a completed event before now.
Bis marks an endpoint; während + genitive describes duration within an event.

reference_content.coverage: Every topic in topic_catalog is rendered from this JSON with a rule, form, explanation notes, common error, memory aid, and up to two rule-linked worked examples from cards.
teaching_order: Decide the meaning or communicative job.
Choose the construction and its word-order or inflection pattern.
Check the common error before producing the sentence.
Study a worked example, then practise the same rule.
reference_content.worked_example_selection: Select up to two cards whose topic_id or rule_ids contains the current topic. Each worked example exposes the prompt, answer, and explanation_en already reviewed with the card.
reference_content.editorial_standard: A topic must never be presented only as a label or a bare formula. Every reference page must connect meaning, form, a frequent error, and a concrete application.

topic_unlock.rule: unlock after two correct basic answers for the topic
unlock after two correct intermediate answers for the topic

ordering: weak-topic cards at the learner's unlocked level

mastery_thresholds.learning: fewer than 3 attempts or accuracy below 60%
mastery_thresholds.developing: at least 3 attempts and accuracy from 60% to 79%
mastery_thresholds.secure: at least 5 attempts, accuracy at least 80%, and one correct production card
mastery_thresholds.mastered: at least 8 attempts, accuracy at least 90%, and two correct advanced or production cards on different days

lapse_rules: After an incorrect answer, show rule_en, form, common_error, and the card explanation.
Repeat the failed card at the end of the same session.
Schedule it again the next day and include one different card from the same topic.
After two consecutive errors, temporarily step down one difficulty level.
rotation_rules: Do not show the same prompt twice in one session unless it was answered incorrectly.
Keep at least 30% of each session as production: transform, reorder, or error_correction.
Once a topic is secure, interleave it with two unrelated topics.
In weeks 11 and 12, hide topic labels and rule hints until after the answer.

exam_readiness_gates.note: These gates measure practice readiness; they do not guarantee an examination result.
grammar_bank: Complete every topic at all three difficulty levels.
Reach at least 80% rolling accuracy in every core topic.
Reach at least 75% rolling accuracy in every supporting topic.
Answer at least two advanced or production cards correctly per topic on different days.
mixed_decks: Score at least 85% on three full mixed decks completed without hints.
Finish each deck within its time limit.
After each deck, correct every error and state the relevant rule without looking.
writing: Complete three 30-minute transfer tasks on different days.
Cover every content point and maintain appropriate register.
Use at least five connectors with correct clause word order.
Leave no repeated case, verb-position, or agreement error after self-correction.
speaking: Complete three partner-style tasks within four minutes each.
Make proposals, justify opinions, respond, and reach a conclusion.
Use at least one subordinate clause, one contrast, and one polite Konjunktiv II form accurately.
Recover from a grammar mistake by reformulating without abandoning the turn.
final_week: Alternate grammar-bank days with complete official telc mock-exam sections.
Do not learn new grammar in the final two days; review only repeated errors and useful sentence frames.

spacing_guidance.again: review in the same session and the next day

weekly_routine: Days 1-4: learn and review the week's grammar cards.
Day 5: mixed Sprachbausteine practice without topic labels.
Day 6: answer production cards aloud and write a short connected text using three target structures.
Day 7: rest or review only cards marked again/hard.
